According to the Health Bulletin 2023, occupancy rates at the 20 least-used UHCs ranged from 11 to 65 percent, while those at the 20 most heavily burdened facilities stood between 160 and 221 percent.
However, upgrading all UHCs to 151 beds, regardless of their individual needs, overlooks significant differences in population, disease burden, location, and existing healthcare capacity.

According to a report by this daily, the three-year project, scheduled to begin in December 2026, will involve constructing new hospital buildings, replacing dilapidated structures, and renovating existing facilities across 443 upazilas.

articles.title: Beyond BNP-AL rivalries, the search for a new political path
articles.excerpt: Politics in Bangladesh is like a vast river at twilight. From afar, it may appear tranquil and unchanging.
articles.fullText:
For decades, two political forces stood upon the opposing banks of this river. On one side stood Awami League, now barred from political activities; on the other, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), now the ruling party. Much of Bangladesh’s political history since independence has been written around these two parties. Parliamentary debates, contested elections, street agitations, mass movements, and even the political arguments of ordinary households have often revolved around these rival poles.

They were adversaries, each other’s fiercest critics, and the principal actors in the recurring drama of power and opposition. Ironically, each party, in a sense, has depended upon the existence of the other. Like day and night, they were opposites that derived meaning and relevance from their contrast. The two parties also defined the boundaries within which Bangladesh’s political life took place.

History, however, is never static. The mass uprising of 2024, the dramatic political transformations that followed, and the subsequent exclusion of Awami League from active politics have thrust Bangladesh into one of the most consequential turning points in its post-independence history. What becomes of a political order when one of its defining pillars is absent? What happens to a nation long accustomed to a political duopoly when the balance is broken?

The conflict between Awami League and BNP was never about elections alone, but also a contest over history. Who was the “legitimate heir” to the Liberation War? How should the nation define itself? What relationship should exist between religion and the state? What should be Bangladesh’s place in the region? Over time, political competition evolved into ideological confrontation. Ideological confrontation, in turn, hardened into mutual suspicion. Eventually, suspicion became a struggle for survival. The tragedy of Bangladesh’s democracy lies partly in this transformation of the two parties’ relationship.

Political opponents in our part of the world often view each other as existential threats. As a consequence, elections cease to be routine democratic exercises and become high-stakes battles in which defeat appears catastrophic and victory absolute. Compromise can be seen as weakness, while restraint may prove to be politically costly.

Following the restoration of parliamentary democracy in 1991, Bangladesh entered an era where power alternated between Awami League and BNP. Other parties existed, some of whom exercised influence and even played important roles in coalition-building. But the centre of gravity remained firmly fixed between BNP and Awami League.

This arrangement brought a certain predictability as citizens knew that governments could change. No party appeared invincible, no electoral victory seemed permanent. But rivalry between the two parties gradually expanded beyond politics into institutions, bureaucracy, academia, and civil society. Public institutions increasingly found themselves drawn into partisan conflicts. Trust became scarce. Consensus became elusive. The state itself sometimes appeared caught in the struggle between competing political narratives.

Awami League occupies a unique place in Bangladesh’s history; its roots stretch into the struggles that shaped modern political consciousness in the country. The party played a profound role in the Language Movement, the Six-Point Movement, the Mass Uprising of 1969 and, ultimately, in the Liberation War. For generations, it was not merely a political party, but also a historical symbol.

Of course, history offers no permanent immunity. The same party that once embodied the aspirations of a people later became the subject of growing criticism. Years of uninterrupted power brought authoritarian tendencies, shrinking democratic space, weakening opposition politics, and an increasing concentration of authority. Whether one accepts or rejects these criticisms, they accumulated over time.

Like many upheavals in history, the July 2024 uprising appeared sudden, but was built upon years of tension, frustration, and unresolved contradictions. The resulting transformation marked not simply the fall of a government, but the collapse of a political equilibrium that had endured for decades.

At first glance, the weakening of its principal rival might appear an enormous opportunity for BNP. History, however, suggests otherwise. For opposition parties, power often seems simpler from a distance. Democracy is easy to defend when one is excluded from authority. Institutional neutrality is easy to demand when one does not control the institutions. Transparency is easy to advocate when one is not responsible for governing. Now in power, BNP faces a challenge that transcends electoral politics. Can it avoid repeating the patterns that it once criticised? Can it strengthen institutions rather than merely occupy them? Can it demonstrate that political power can be exercised without reproducing the same cycles of domination and exclusion?

Political parties can be weakened, banned, and/or marginalised. But they rarely disappear completely. Jamaat-e-Islami is a glaring example of the same.

Awami League’s legacy is woven deeply into the political fabric of Bangladesh. For that reason, its absence from formal politics does not automatically erase its presence from public life. The future may therefore bring reinvention, fragmentation, or transformation under new leadership or in a different form.

A younger generation has emerged whose concerns differ significantly from those of earlier decades. For many young citizens, old ideological battles hold less emotional power than they once did. Their priorities are more immediate: employment, education, merit-based opportunities, transparency, efficient governance, freedom of expression, economic mobility, and so forth. This generation did not live through the foundational conflicts of earlier eras. It inherited their consequences but not necessarily their loyalties. As a result, the politics of the future may not revolve exclusively around the historic Awami League-BNP divide. Instead, it may increasingly revolve around a set of questions: who governs effectively? Who combats corruption? Who delivers opportunities? Who protects freedom? Who builds institutions capable of outlasting individuals?

Nations mature when they learn from their own history, and Bangladesh’s recent decades can offer powerful lessons for our politicians. Unchecked political dominance creates distortions. But the complete absence of meaningful competition creates dangers of its own. Perhaps what Bangladesh now requires is not a new political arrangement, but a new covenant; a shared understanding that political rivals are not enemies. That elections should not determine who “owns” the state. That political defeat should not mean political extinction. That institutions must be stronger than personalities. Such transformations are never easy as they demand patience, wisdom, restraint, and virtues not traditionally found in our politics. But without them, the cycle of confrontation risks perpetuating itself indefinitely.

The old political order may not return. New actors have emerged. Fresh alignments are also taking shape. The entire structure of political competition may evolve into something unrecognisable to earlier generations. But one truth remains: the future of Bangladesh cannot be determined by any single party or leader. It will be determined by the resilience of institutions, the wisdom of citizens, and the nation’s ability to reconcile freedom with stability.

Mohiuddin Ahmad is a writer and researcher of Bangladesh’s political history.

articles.title: Chattogram's expansion into flood-prone areas is a dangerous gamble
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s main seaport is in Chattogram, a sprawling metropolis endowed with the distinct natural features of hills, rivers and the sea.
articles.fullText:
Findings from the Asian Development Bank’s (ADB) Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026, reported by The Daily Star on October 22, serve as a fresh warning. According to the report, Chattogram’s built-up area spanned 66.1 square kilometres in 2016, expanding to 73.5 square kilometres by 2025. Over this period, settlements and infrastructure in flood-prone zones grew by 16.2 percent, compared to a 9.7 percent growth rate on safer land. What’s most alarming is that expansion has been fastest in the city’s most vulnerable areas. The report noted that nearly a quarter of Chattogram’s built-up area is at risk of inundation from severe coastal flooding. In other words, the city is not just expanding; a significant portion of this growth is occurring in areas where coastal floodwaters could reach hazardous levels in the future.

Waterlogging has been a particularly troubling problem in recent years. A combination of heavy rainfall, runoff from the hills, tidal water, inadequate drainage systems, and encroachment on canals and drains makes life extremely difficult during the monsoon. However, seeing it as simply an issue of cleaning drains and canals would leave the root cause unaddressed. A city’s natural waterways, low-lying retention basins, ponds, wetlands, and open spaces temporarily hold rainwater. When these areas are filled up to build roads and structures, the soil’s capacity to absorb rainwater diminishes. At the same time, natural runoff is restricted, quickly overwhelming the drainage system with massive volumes of water within a short period.

The crisis is further aggravated by hill-cutting, silt accumulation in canals, canal encroachment, unplanned road elevation, and utility infrastructure obstructing water flow. During high tides, rising river and canal levels also prevent rainwater from draining out. When combined with heavy rainfall, these factors make waterlogging particularly devastating.

In various parts of Chattogram, residential and commercial structures have been built on natural water bodies and low-lying areas. Questions have been raised about changes in land use in several areas, including Anannya Residential Area, Kulgaon, Baluchhara, and Jalalabad. Reports have also highlighted encroachment and illegal structures around the Chaktai canal, Mirza canal, Manoharkhali canal, and the Kalirchhara canal. Similarly, development activities along the banks of the Karnaphuli River have again raised concerns about the natural waterways and environmental constraints.

It is important to realise that approval from a housing or infrastructure development authority does not automatically make a project environmentally safe. The soundness of a plan depends on whether it takes into account the nature of the land, drainage routes, the need to preserve water bodies, and future flood risks. These are precisely the criteria against which questions can be, and have been, raised about the filling up of water bodies and low-lying areas in the Chattogram Development Authority’s (CDA) own Anannya Residential Project. Therefore, the CDA’s projects must also be assessed against the same environmental standards.

Plans exist, but where is the implementation?

The CDA’s 1995 Stormwater Drainage and Flood Control Master Plan identified various drainage and waterlogging challenges, offering recommendations on where water would accumulate, which routes it should drain through, and where retention ponds were needed. But identifying problems is one thing; resolving them on the ground is another. Multiple projects are currently underway to alleviate waterlogging in Chattogram, and substantial funds are being spent on re-excavating, widening and renovating canals, digging new ones, and constructing flood control infrastructure. While the necessity of these initiatives is undeniable, a closer review of their planning, design and execution reveals several fundamental shortcomings.

First, out of the city’s 104 identified canals, ongoing projects cover only 36. As a result, a large part of the overall drainage network remains outside their scope, even though the effectiveness of any canal depends on its connected upstream channels, tributaries, and adjoining drains. Second, 12 proposed silt traps were dropped due to funding constraints and cost-cutting measures. Given the heavy runoff of sand and silt from the hills into the canals, silt traps are vital. Dropping them risks silting up the re-excavated canals within a short period.

Third, the 1995 master plan recommended constructing retention ponds or temporary water reservoirs in the city’s low-lying areas. When heavy rainfall coincides with high tides, the drainage of water into rivers and canals is obstructed. In such situations, retention ponds are indispensable for temporarily holding excess runoff. But the ongoing projects have virtually ignored the construction and preservation of such reservoirs. This is a major planning flaw.

Fourth, the natural width of some canals has been reduced during the construction of regulators, potentially obstructing the normal flow of water. Similarly, questions have been raised about plans to install fewer pumps than necessary or pumps with insufficient capacity. It is urgent to reassess whether these pumps will be able to drain sufficient amounts of water during heavy rainfall combined with high tides.

Fifth, faulty designs and infrastructure at certain locations are obstructing water flow through canals. Examples include the construction of two-way box culverts over the Hijra canal in Panchlaish, opposite the medical college, and the Shital Jharna canal near the entrance to Chattogram Cantonment Public School and College. The partition wall in the middle of these culverts could trap waste and obstruct water flow. Such obstructions further reduce drainage capacity, particularly during heavy rainfall. In addition, there are persistent problems with disconnected canal networks, improperly graded bed levels and flow directions, and obstructions created by utility pipelines and other structures.

Another issue is the piecemeal tendency to raise road levels to combat waterlogging. In many cases, roads have been elevated without factoring in the height of adjoining drains and properties, leaving houses and shops lower than the street. As a result, even light rainfall causes overflow or seepage from drains to enter these properties.

There have also been instances of poor coordination during project implementation. Temporary embankments or barriers have reportedly been constructed at the mouths of the Hijra and Jamalkhan canals to facilitate construction work, obstructing water drainage. Meanwhile, the exchange of accusations between the city corporation and the CDA over canal cleaning, drainage connections, and obstructions caused by construction work highlights the lack of coordination in project implementation. Such disputes are unacceptable when it comes to an integrated task like resolving waterlogging.

Finally, clear arrangements must be made to ensure that the completed canals, regulators, pumps, and silt traps can be effectively operated and maintained, with adequate institutional responsibility and capacity. Without dedicated manpower, equipment, funding, and a clear operations and maintenance manual, sustaining these structures over the long term will be impossible.

Need for an integrated, science-based approach

To protect Chattogram, it is not enough to just drain water after waterlogging occurs. Questions of where water will accumulate, which paths it will take, and which areas are safe for human settlement and infrastructure must be resolved at the very beginning of development planning.

First, a comprehensive flood risk map must be prepared for Chattogram and its expanding peripheries, identifying potential flood depths, water flow routes, water bodies, low-lying areas, hill runoff, and tidal surges. Second, independent experts must review the ongoing projects and designs. Necessary steps must be taken to restore dropped canals and silt traps, build retention ponds, correct regulator and pump capacities, fix culvert flaws, and complete missing canal connections.

Third, canals, ponds, wetlands, and low-lying retention basins must be surveyed, demarcated, and legally protected. Stringent action should be taken against illegal encroachment and land-filling. Fourth, the responsibilities of the CDA, Chittagong City Corporation, Bangladesh Water Development Board, port authority, and utility agencies must be clearly defined by law, with effective coordination mechanisms. A single capable agency should oversee drainage operations and maintenance.

Fifth, planned satellite towns should be developed in neighbouring upazilas to ease demographic and infrastructural pressure on the city. Expanding employment, education, healthcare and public transit in those areas would eliminate the need for people to settle in vulnerable low-lying urban areas.

As much of the country’s import and export trade passes through Chattogram port, the city’s climate resilience is vital not just to the national economy but also to its residents. Urban expansion may be inevitable, but unplanned growth across floodplains is not. The authorities concerned must ensure that today’s development does not become tomorrow’s disaster.

Md Delwar Hossain Mazumdar is former chairman of the Institution of Engineers, Bangladesh (IEB), Chattogram Centre, and treasurer at Forum for Planned Chittagong.

articles.title: নিবর্তনমূলক ধারাগুলো বাদ দিতে হবে
articles.excerpt: গুজবের সংজ্ঞা থেকে ‘অসমর্থিত তথ্য’ বাদ দিয়ে ইচ্ছাকৃত মিথ্যা বা বিকৃত তথ্য প্রচারের বিষয়টিকে গুরুত্ব দেওয়া হয়েছে।
articles.fullText: সাইবার সুরক্ষা আইন সংশোধনের নতুন খসড়ায় কয়েকটি অপরাধের শাস্তি কমানো এবং নিবন্ধিত সংবাদমাধ্যমের জন্য কিছু সুরক্ষার প্রস্তাব এসেছে। অংশীজনদের সঙ্গে আলোচনা করে খসড়া সংশোধন ও আবার জনমতের জন্য প্রকাশ করা ইতিবাচক উদ্যোগ। কিন্তু একটি আইনের গ্রহণযোগ্যতা শুধু শাস্তির মেয়াদ দিয়ে বিচার করা যায় না। কোন কাজকে অপরাধ হিসেবে গণ্য করা হচ্ছে, তার সংজ্ঞা কতটা সুনির্দিষ্ট এবং আইন প্রয়োগকারী সংস্থাকে কতটা ক্ষমতা দেওয়া হচ্ছে—এসবই মূল বিবেচ্য। সেই বিচারে নতুন খসড়াতেও উদ্বেগের যথেষ্ট কারণ রয়েছে। গুজব ও অপতথ্য প্রচারের সর্বোচ্চ কারাদণ্ড ১০ বছর থেকে ৫ বছর এবং মানহানির শাস্তি ৫ বছর থেকে ২ বছর করার প্রস্তাব রয়েছে। জরিমানাও কমানো হচ্ছে। কিন্তু সমালোচনা বা ব্যঙ্গের জন্য কাউকে ফৌজদারি মামলার মুখোমুখি করার সুযোগ থাকলে শাস্তি কমানো কোনো বড় পরিবর্তন আনবে না। মামলা, গ্রেপ্তার, জামিনের অনিশ্চয়তা ও দীর্ঘ বিচারপ্রক্রিয়াই একজন মানুষের জন্য শাস্তি হয়ে উঠতে পারে। ফলে আইনের নিবর্তনমূলক চরিত্র বদলাতে হলে অপরাধের তালিকা ও সংজ্ঞাতেই মৌলিক পরিবর্তন প্রয়োজন। গুজবের সংজ্ঞা থেকে ‘অসমর্থিত তথ্য’ বাদ দিয়ে ইচ্ছাকৃত মিথ্যা বা বিকৃত তথ্য প্রচারের বিষয়টিকে গুরুত্ব দেওয়া হয়েছে। এটি কিছুটা অগ্রগতি। তবে ‘উত্তেজনা’ কিংবা ‘সামাজিক অস্থিরতা’ সৃষ্টির মতো শব্দের প্রয়োগ কীভাবে হবে, সেই প্রশ্ন থাকছে। সরকারের ব্যর্থতা বা অনিয়মের খবরেও জনমনে ক্ষোভ তৈরি হতে পারে। সেই প্রতিক্রিয়াকে অপরাধের ভিত্তি বানানোর সুযোগ রাখা চলবে না। ইচ্ছাকৃত প্রতারণা বা সহিংসতায় সরাসরি উসকানির সঙ্গে সংবাদ, মতামত ও সমালোচনার পার্থক্য স্পষ্ট করতে হবে। মানহানির সংজ্ঞায় ‘গঠনমূলক সমালোচনার সীমা’ অতিক্রমের কথা আরও উদ্বেগজনক। কোন সমালোচনা গঠনমূলক, তা নির্ধারণ করবে কে? সমালোচনা গ্রহণের শর্ত কি সংশ্লিষ্ট ব্যক্তির সন্তুষ্টি হবে? মিম, ব্যঙ্গচিত্র বা ক্যারিকেচারকে উপহাসের যুক্তিতে অপরাধের আওতায় আনার সুযোগ থাকলে রাজনৈতিক ব্যঙ্গও ঝুঁকিতে পড়বে। চেহারা বা শারীরিক বৈশিষ্ট্য নিয়ে অবমাননা অবশ্যই নিন্দনীয়। কিন্তু তা প্রতিকারের বিধান যেন ক্ষমতাবানদের সমালোচনা থেকে রক্ষার ঢাল না হয়। মানহানির জন্য কারাদণ্ডের বিধান বাদ দিয়ে উপযুক্ত দেওয়ানি প্রতিকারের ব্যবস্থা করাই বাঞ্ছনীয়। নিবন্ধিত সংবাদমাধ্যমে প্রকাশিত কনটেন্টের কারণে গ্রেপ্তারের আগে ট্রাইব্যুনালের অনুমতি এবং মামলা শুরুর আগে আত্মপক্ষ সমর্থনের সুযোগ দেওয়ার প্রস্তাব স্বস্তিদায়ক। কিন্তু মতপ্রকাশের স্বাধীনতা কেবল নিবন্ধিত প্রতিষ্ঠানের অধিকার নয়; ফ্রিল্যান্স সাংবাদিক, স্বাধীন লেখক ও সাধারণ নাগরিকের জন্যও সমান সুরক্ষা প্রয়োজন। সংবাদমাধ্যমের নিবন্ধন নাগরিক অধিকারের মানদণ্ড হতে পারে না। পাশাপাশি সংবাদকক্ষে তল্লাশি ও সাংবাদিকদের যন্ত্রপাতি জব্দের ক্ষেত্রেও কার্যকর বিচারিক সুরক্ষা থাকতে হবে; নইলে সংবাদসূত্রের গোপনীয়তা বিপন্ন হবে। কনটেন্ট অপসারণের ক্ষেত্রে ‘দেশের মর্যাদা’ ও ‘জনশৃঙ্খলা’র মতো অস্পষ্ট শব্দ প্রশাসনকে ব্যাপক ক্ষমতা দিতে পারে। অপসারণের সিদ্ধান্তের সময়ই কারণ জানানো, দ্রুত আপিল এবং স্বাধীন বিচারিক পর্যালোচনার সুযোগ নিশ্চিত করা প্রয়োজন। একইভাবে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ তথ্য পরিকাঠামোয় হামলার ক্ষেত্রে প্রমাণ রক্ষার জরুরি প্রয়োজন থাকলেও বিনা পরোয়ানায় তল্লাশি, জব্দ ও গ্রেপ্তারের ক্ষমতা কঠোর শর্ত ও দ্রুত বিচারিক পর্যালোচনার অধীন রাখতে হবে। ডিজিটাল নিরাপত্তা আইন ভিন্নমত দমনের হাতিয়ার হওয়ার অভিজ্ঞতা আমাদের সামনে রয়েছে। নাম বদল বা শাস্তি হ্রাসের মাধ্যমে সেই ব্যবস্থার পুনরাবৃত্তি গ্রহণযোগ্য নয়। সরকারকে অংশীজনদের মৌলিক আপত্তিগুলো আমলে নিতে হবে। সাইবার অপরাধ প্রতিরোধের আইনে মানহানি, ব্যঙ্গ ও অস্পষ্টভাবে সংজ্ঞায়িত গুজবকে ফৌজদারি অপরাধ হিসেবে রাখার বিধান বাদ দিতে হবে। এ আইনের লক্ষ্য হোক সমালোচকদের মুখ বন্ধ করা নয়, মানুষের ডিজিটাল নিরাপত্তা নিশ্চিত করা।

articles.title: প্রতিরোধে প্রশাসনিক উদ্যোগই যথেষ্ট নয়
articles.excerpt: বাংলাদেশ পরিসংখ্যান ব্যুরো (বিবিএস) ও ইউনিসেফের সর্বশেষ জরিপ বলছে, দেশে বাল্যবিবাহের হার কিছুটা কমার চিত্র পাওয়া গেছে।
articles.fullText: বাল্যবিবাহ প্রতিরোধে বাংলাদেশে আইন আছে, সরকারি-বেসরকারি নানা উদ্যোগও রয়েছে। সচেতনতা তৈরিতে প্রচার-প্রচারণা চলছে। কিন্তু বাস্তবতা হলো এসব উদ্যোগের পরও বাল্যবিবাহের প্রবণতা থামানো যাচ্ছে না। ৯ মাসে সাতক্ষীরায় ১৩২টি বাল্যবিবাহ বন্ধ করার তথ্য জানিয়েছে প্রশাসন। এক দশক আগে ঘটা করে কালীগঞ্জকে বাল্যবিবাহমুক্ত উপজেলা ঘোষণা করা হয়েছিল। অথচ সেই উপজেলাতেই গত ছয় মাসে ১১টি বাল্যবিবাহ প্রতিরোধ করতে হয়েছে। এর বাইরে কতটি বাল্যবিবাহ সংঘটিত হয়েছে, তার হিসাবও নেই। এ চিত্র শুধু একটি উপজেলার নয়, বাল্যবিবাহ প্রতিরোধে প্রশাসনের সামগ্রিক উদ্যোগের দুর্বলতাও তুলে ধরে। প্রথম আলো র খবর জানাচ্ছে, জানাজানি হলে প্রশাসন বাধা দিতে পারে, এমন আশঙ্কায় গোপনে বাল্যবিবাহের আয়োজন করে থাকেন অভিভাবকেরা। বিয়ের পর মেয়েকে শ্বশুরবাড়ি না পাঠিয়ে কিছুদিন পর পাঠানো হয়। বাংলাদেশ পরিসংখ্যান ব্যুরো (বিবিএস) ও ইউনিসেফের সর্বশেষ জরিপ বলছে, দেশে বাল্যবিবাহের হার কিছুটা কমার চিত্র পাওয়া গেছে। ২০১৯ সালে ২০-২৪ বছর বয়সী নারীদের মধ্যে ১৮ বছরের আগে বিয়ের হার ছিল ৫১ দশমিক ৪ শতাংশ, ২০২৫ সালে তা কমে ৪৭ দশমিক ২ শতাংশ হয়েছে। কিন্তু এই অগ্রগতিতে সন্তুষ্ট হওয়ার সুযোগ নেই। কেননা এখনো দেশের প্রায় অর্ধেক মেয়ের বিয়ে হচ্ছে ১৮ বছর পূর্ণ হওয়ার আগে। বাল্যবিবাহ একটি মেয়ের শৈশব, শিক্ষা ও সম্ভাবনাকে কেড়ে নেয়। অল্প বয়সে গর্ভধারণ মা ও শিশুর স্বাস্থ্যঝুঁকি বাড়ায়। প্রসবজনিত জটিলতা, মাতৃমৃত্যু ও অপুষ্টির ঝুঁকিও তৈরি হয়। অপ্রাপ্তবয়স্ক মেয়েরা সংসারের দায়িত্ব নিতে গিয়ে শিক্ষা থেকে ঝরে পড়ে। অর্থনৈতিকভাবে স্বাবলম্বী হওয়ার সুযোগ হারায়। অনেক ক্ষেত্রে নির্যাতন ও বৈষম্যের শিকার হয়। অর্থাৎ বাল্যবিবাহ শুধু একটি মেয়ের জীবনকেই ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত করে না, দারিদ্র্য ও অসমতার চক্রকেও দীর্ঘস্থায়ী করে। দেশের মানবসম্পদ উন্নয়ন ও নারীর সমান অধিকার প্রতিষ্ঠার স্বার্থেও বাল্যবিবাহ প্রতিরোধ জরুরি। প্রথম আলো র প্রতিবেদনে বাল্যবিবাহের পেছনে মেয়েদের নিরাপত্তা নিয়ে অভিভাবকদের উদ্বেগ, প্রেমের সম্পর্ক, আর্থিক অসচ্ছলতা ও সামাজিক চাপের কথা উঠে এসেছে। এসব কারণ উপেক্ষা করে শুধু অভিভাবকদের কাছ থেকে মুচলেকা নেওয়া কিংবা জরিমানা করে এই সমস্যার স্থায়ী সমাধান সম্ভব নয়। একই সঙ্গে বিয়ের আয়োজনের সঙ্গে যুক্ত মধ্যস্থতাকারী, ভুয়া নিকাহ রেজিস্ট্রার ও অসাধু কাজিদেরও আইনের আওতায় আনতে হবে। আমরা মনে করি, জন্মনিবন্ধন যাচাই ছাড়া বিয়ের নিবন্ধন বন্ধ করতে হবে। একই সঙ্গে বিদ্যালয় ও মাদ্রাসাভিত্তিক নজরদারি জোরদার করা জরুরি। কোনো ছাত্রী হঠাৎ অনুপস্থিত হলে তার কারণ অনুসন্ধান করতে হবে। বাল্যবিবাহপ্রবণ এলাকায় স্থানীয় জনপ্রতিনিধি, শিক্ষক, ধর্মীয় নেতা, নারী সংগঠন ও প্রশাসনের সমন্বয়ে বাল্যবিবাহ প্রতিরোধ কমিটি গড়ে তোলা জরুরি। একই সঙ্গে মেয়েদের শিক্ষা, বৃত্তি, কারিগরি প্রশিক্ষণ ও কর্মসংস্থানের সুযোগ বাড়াতে হবে। অভিভাবকদের অর্থনৈতিক দুশ্চিন্তা দূর করাও জরুরি। শুধু প্রশাসনিক উদ্যোগ নয়, বাল্যবিবাহ বন্ধে প্রয়োজন সমন্বিত পদক্ষেপ।

How can we make healthcare decentralisation work? Lessons from an upazila-level project
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s overall health workforce density remains below the recommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO), with pronounced rural-urban imbalances.
articles.fullText:
The Upazila Governance and Development Project (UGDP), implemented by the Local Government Division (LGD) under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, represented a bold bet on decentralisation. Launched in FY2015-16 and completed on December 31, 2025, UGDP strengthened upazila parishads through performance-based financing, capacity development, and targeted infrastructure and service-delivery sub-projects. High-performing upazilas received additional funds, typically Tk 50 lakh per year on top of the upazila Annual Development Programme (ADP) block allocation from the government.

Under the project, more than 47,000 medical works, items, and supplies were delivered across 408 upazilas. Later, assessment of 158 upazilas showed that 91.88 percent of the 29,257 items distributed there are currently operational and actively serving patients—far better than many comparable public infrastructure initiatives. The upazilas invested over Tk 113 crore in obtaining diagnostic tools, upgrading facilities, and addressing local gaps through decentralised procurement that proved faster and more responsive than traditional centralised systems. This success validated the core idea: when local governments are empowered with funds and authority, they can tailor solutions to real community needs, fostering a stronger sense of ownership.

However, the same assessment also exposed systemic “structural friction” that threatens long-term sustainability. In the 158 upazilas covered under the study, approximately 8.11 percent (2,375 out of 29,257 units) of equipment were non-functional or underutilised, not primarily due to manufacturing defects, but because of deep mismatches between hardware provision and the human, financial and logistical systems managed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

Media often reported on high-tech anaesthesia machines sitting idle in facilities lacking sanctioned junior anaesthesia consultants; X-ray and ultrasonography units gathering dust without radiologists; ambulances delivered without trained drivers or dedicated fuel budgets, etc. Minor faults escalate into full breakdowns because local managers have no quick-access “emergency repair fund” and must navigate lengthy central approvals. Diagnostic equipment often becomes inoperable once initial stocks of reagents, films, or consumables run out, with no flexible local budget to replenish them. These issues mirror broader, well-documented challenges in our rural health system: chronic workforce shortages (with over half of physician posts at many UHCs vacant in some divisions); high workloads on existing staff; and rigid financial rules that hinder timely maintenance.

Besides, Bangladesh’s overall health workforce density remains below the recommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO), with pronounced rural-urban imbalances. Doctors and specialists gravitate towards cities, leaving remote upazilas struggling. Even when equipment arrives, the absence of matching specialists creates “deadweight loss.” Studies using Workload Indicators of Staffing Need (WISN) confirm that physicians and nurses at UHCs often operate under very high workload pressure, yet sanctioned posts frequently go unfilled, exacerbating inefficiencies.

Maintenance and supply chain gaps compound the problem. Small repairs (under Tk 20,000) can sideline machines for months. Consumables exhaustion turns sophisticated diagnostics into expensive paperweights. Logistical oversights, such as generators without fuel allocations, further erode returns on investment. These frictions risk turning hundreds of crores of taka in public assets into depreciating liabilities, eroding public trust, and driving more referrals to already overburdened district and tertiary hospitals.

To transform the infrastructure victories achieved under the UGDP into a durable, self-sustaining ecosystem, Bangladesh must move beyond ad-hoc procurement and embrace a roadmap defined by inter-ministerial integration and local autonomy. At first, the “No Staff, No Stuff” mandate must be enforced. We must stop delivering sophisticated hardware to facilities that lack the specialists to use them. The procurement of specialised equipment must be strictly synchronised with human resource deployment. This requires a Joint Human Resource Mapping Protocol between the health and LGRD ministries to ensure that infrastructure sub-projects are only approved when the necessary specialists are either already on site or are part of a firm, imminent recruitment timeline. This must be paired with aggressive rural retention incentives, such as hardship allowances, improved housing, and faster career progression, so that our best medical minds are willing to serve in the heartlands where they are needed most.

Simultaneously, we must address rigid financial rules that turn minor mechanical issues into long-term breakdowns. Currently, a small repair costing less than Tk 20,000 can sideline a vital machine for months while local managers navigate the labyrinth of central approvals. We must grant our local facilities the breathing room to act swiftly. By authorising upazila parishads to ring-fence a portion of income generated from diagnostic services using UGDP-provided equipment, they can be empowered to handle on-site fixes and utility needs without delay. This would also create a self-sustaining cycle of care and accountability.

Moreover, future procurement contracts must be smarter and more comprehensive, mandating the bundling of a full year’s supply of consumables and long-term warranties that shift the maintenance burden upstream to the vendors. By integrating this equipment into the National Essential Drug and Supply List, their replenishment can be ensured through established, reliable channels rather than through desperate, ad-hoc local efforts.

Finally, we must institutionalise operational readiness. No high-value asset, be it an ambulance or a generator, should be handed over without a formal verification that the facility is ready to use it. This means having a designated operator, a ring-fenced fuel budget, and a clear maintenance plan in place before the keys are turned over.

The stakes of this transition are incredibly high. If we fail to act, hundreds of crores of taka in public assets may gradually turn into depreciating liabilities. Public trust will erode as communities find that modern facilities and equipment, intended for their benefit, remain inaccessible. Such inaction will inevitably increase overcrowding at already burdened district and tertiary hospitals, slowing our progress towards universal health coverage.

However, decisive action to bridge the gap between infrastructure provision and operational sustainability could transform the lessons of UGDP into a model of global excellence. With the second phase of UGDP (UGDP-2) pledged during the prime minister’s visit to Japan, this is the right time to review the project’s achievements and challenges and incorporate those lessons into UGDP-2’s design. While no single project can transform the healthcare system overnight, careful project design and implementation can build on past successes, address existing shortcomings, and deliver greater and more sustainable impact.

Dr Syed Abdul Hamid is professor at the Institute of Health Economics of the University of Dhaka.

Corruption can’t be dressed up as gifts
articles.excerpt: The LGRD state minister’s remark on bribes sends the wrong signal.
articles.fullText:
It is indeed shocking that the state minister, speaking at a public event , said if a contractor, “being satisfied, gives the engineer a gift from his profit, that does not fall under the category of bribery.” This remark cannot be dismissed as offhand—even though the state minister has apologised and withdrawn it —nor does his explanation that he was speaking informally absolve him of his responsibility. The LGRD ministry's defence of the remark is also troubling. Engineers are paid by the state to ensure the quality of public works, certify completed projects, and clear bills in accordance with the rules. Taking gifts from contractors is a clear violation of restrictions on such benefits under the Penal Code as well as government conduct rules, as TIB rightly pointed out .

We are also surprised at the lack of a public statement from the government to distance itself from such a controversial remark. Nor has there been, as of this writing, any reaction from the parliament floor. What does it say about the reality of graft culture in our country?

Our indignation is rooted in numbers. TIB's National Household Survey 2025 on corruption prevalence found that 81.6 percent of households experienced corruption while accessing public services, while 63.6 percent were compelled to pay bribes. The estimated value of bribe transactions around the country reached Tk 12,633.2 crore in 2025. These numbers represent citizens paying extra for services to which they are entitled, often because they have no meaningful alternative. The Anti-Corruption Commission, too, has fallen short in its role as the primary graft watchdog. TIB found that only 0.3 percent of survey respondents had lodged complaints with the ACC, pointing to a serious trust deficit.

This is not an isolated incident. Earlier in February, only days after taking office, Road Transport Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam argued that collections from transport operators were not extortion if made through mutual understanding . Can one really doubt that such attempts to redefine questionable practices weaken the government's credibility? We resent Shahe Alam’s remark and expect more responsible, measured public speaking from our government officials. On its part, the government must publicly reaffirm that corruption cannot be excused under any circumstances, and strengthen the institutions meant to tackle it. If the government wants people to put their trust in its capabilities, it must match its anti-graft pledge with consistent action.

articles.title: We must prioritise RSV prevention to strengthen pneumonia control
articles.excerpt: A study published in The Lancet Global Health last year, conducted from January to December 2019 at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, found RSV in 21 percent of children hospitalised with suspected respiratory infections who were tested
articles.fullText:
One often overlooked but important contributor is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a leading viral cause of pneumonia and bronchiolitis, particularly during the first few months of life. Although most infections are mild, severe RSV infection can cause breathing difficulties, respiratory failure, and even death. Bangladesh already protects children against important bacterial causes of pneumonia through routine immunisation, but RSV remains a significant gap in prevention.

Local evidence demonstrates the magnitude of this burden. A study published in The Lancet Global Health last year, conducted from January to December 2019 at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, found RSV in 21 percent of children hospitalised with suspected respiratory infections who were tested. Their median age was just three months, and their median hospital stay was five days. More recent community-based research published in The Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia [SS1] this year provides further evidence. Researchers followed 3,667 children in rural Mirzapur between August 2021 and June 2023 and found that RSV-associated respiratory illness was most frequent during the first six months of life. These outcomes indicate how preventing severe respiratory infections could relieve pressure on hospitals and improve access to lifesaving care for children with other diseases.

Beyond the clinical burden, childhood pneumonia and RSV impose substantial financial hardship on families. A Bangladesh study published in the Journal of Global Health found that more than half of families with children hospitalised for RSV had to borrow money to cover treatment costs, while out-of-pocket expenditure accounted for nearly one quarter of their monthly household income. Together, these studies demonstrate that respiratory syncytial virus places a substantial burden on both communities and hospitals, reinforcing the importance of protection from birth.

Families are also beginning to recognise this need. Following our earlier columns in this daily— “Bangladesh needs a national RSV vaccination strategy” and “Maternal vaccination can close the immunity gap for newborns” —we received inquiries from readers seeking access to the RSV vaccine. One expectant father told us that his wife was around 30 weeks pregnant and that he had searched hospitals and pharmacies without success. He wanted to know where he could find the vaccine. Unfortunately, we had to disappoint him by explaining that it was not yet available in the country, despite advances that now make it possible to protect infants against severe RSV illness.

As the recently concluded RSV Awareness Week (November 2-6) draws attention to the respiratory syncytial virus, World Pneumonia Day on November 12 offers an opportunity to consider how RSV prevention can strengthen Bangladesh's broader pneumonia prevention strategy. The World Health Organization (WHO) now recommends two approaches to protect infants against severe RSV disease: i) maternal vaccination during pregnancy; and ii) long-acting monoclonal antibodies administered directly to infants. Maternal vaccination allows protective antibodies to pass from mother to baby before birth, while monoclonal antibodies, such as nirsevimab, offer another effective option. However, the relatively high price of monoclonal antibodies remains a challenge for resource-constrained healthcare systems. Maternal vaccination offers a potentially practical opportunity to protect infants during their most vulnerable months.

Nonetheless, introducing new preventive interventions requires sustainable financing. Bangladesh must accommodate emerging vaccines while maintaining existing immunisation programmes and responding to growing demands on public health resources. One possibility lies in the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), which the country currently administers through a three-dose schedule. Updated WHO recommendations in 2025 recognise that countries with mature PCV programmes, sustained high coverage, and sufficient population immunity may consider a two-dose schedule, consisting of one primary dose in early infancy and a booster later. Where appropriate, this transition could reduce vaccine procurement requirements and create financial space for additional preventive interventions.

The Every Breath Counts Coalition , a global partnership advocating for the prevention of childhood pneumonia deaths, has launched the STOP RSV initiative to promote awareness and accelerate access to maternal RSV vaccination. The coalition has also proposed that eligible countries consider using potential savings from optimised PCV schedules to support maternal RSV vaccine introduction. Bangladesh is among the countries identified for consideration. This opportunity warrants careful assessment of local disease patterns, vaccination coverage, and programme readiness. PCV and RSV vaccines complement each other, protecting against important bacterial and viral causes of childhood pneumonia.

The Gates Foundation -supported Maternal Immunisation Readiness Network in Africa and Asia (MIRNA) is strengthening preparedness for maternal vaccination in low- and middle-income countries across Asia and Africa. In Bangladesh, MIRNA is generating evidence on RSV burden, vaccine acceptance, cost-effectiveness, and implementation readiness. A recent publication in Health Care Science highlighted the importance of integrating maternal RSV vaccination into antenatal care, strengthening public-private coordination, and addressing implementation and financing challenges.

Bangladesh's immunisation policymakers, technical advisory bodies, and development partners should now evaluate the potential health benefits of RSV prevention, the feasibility of PCV schedule optimisation, and sustainable financing options. Such assessments should consider not only infections and deaths prevented, but also hospitalisations avoided, hospital capacity preserved, and financial burdens reduced for families.

World Pneumonia Day calls for decisive policy action. Bangladesh has an opportunity to prioritise maternal RSV vaccination and establish a clear, sustainable pathway for its introduction.

Aniqa Tasnim Hossain is associate scientist at icddr,b.

Dr Ridwana Maher Manna is study physician at icddr,b.

Dr Ahmed Ehsanur Rahman is scientist at icddr,b.

Dr Shams El Arifeen is senior scientist (emeritus) at icddr,b.

articles.excerpt: Lawmakers must uphold people’s right to cultural expressions
articles.fullText:
What’s worrying is that the cancellation of music, cultural and sporting events, as well as attacks on syncretic religio-cultural traditions, is being normalised here. According to one estimate, since August 2024, at least 36 such events have either been cancelled or faced threats from right-wing religious groups. According to reports, more than 90 shrines have come under attack between August 2024 and February 2026. Police largely remained passive in these cases, neither providing extra protection or security at programme venues, nor arresting those who issued threats or vandalised event sites. Instead, in some instances, they urged the organisers to cancel events, citing security concerns. The November 3 exhibition at the Liberation War Museum is a case in point.

Surprisingly, some of our lawmakers, instead of voicing support for our diverse cultural traditions and national heritage, are enabling attempts to suppress cultural expressions through their statements and instructions. Not everyone may like folk or Baul songs and their practices, but that does not mean programmes featuring such music should be stopped entirely.

Our constitution, in fact, asks the state to ensure that measures are taken to preserve cultural heritage and expressions, that minority communities can practise their faith and tradition without fear, and that people can express their thoughts in various forms, including creative works. Why, then, are we witnessing our lawmakers, who took an oath under that very constitution, act and speak in ways that contradict it? If the BNP is true to its promise of building an inclusive society, its members should first understand its meaning and not instruct the police to cancel cultural events.

articles.title: Why Dhaka doesn’t want Hasina back
articles.excerpt: Seen from Sheikh Hasina’s perspective, deciding to try and return to Bangladesh is clever politics.
articles.fullText:
First, it makes her relevant again; it makes her the centre of the story. Second, it looks brave and self-sacrificing, with her facing imprisonment and possibly even death . Third, it allows her supporters to contrast her “bravery” with that of the current prime minister, Tarique Rahman, who did not attempt to return to Bangladesh and face detention while Awami League was in power.

Fourth, it makes her appear loyal and empathetic towards her Awami League colleagues and supporters, since she suggests she is returning in part because of the rights violations and suffering they now face. Fifth, it will let her and Awami League draw far more critical attention to the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) and the in absentia trial in which she was convicted.

Sixth, and perhaps most importantly, it puts the BNP government in a very difficult position. Officially, the government wants her back to face her sentence. In reality, her return could be the last thing it wants, because it would then have to decide whether to let her execution go ahead or find a way to avoid it, through her appeal or presidential clemency.

There would be huge public demand for her execution. And people would point out that between 2013 and 2016, the Awami League government executed five Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and one BNP leader, all convicted by the same tribunal that has now convicted her.

But the government also knows that Awami League still has considerable support in the country. Executing her could prove explosive, with consequences that are hard to predict and could badly damage both the country and the ruling BNP. Her execution, or even just her being in jail, would almost certainly lead to resurgent Awami League protests resulting in repression and human rights violations as the government tries to contain them.

Then there is the question of who she is. Whatever Hasina’s misdeeds and crimes, can a BNP government really hang the daughter of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the country’s independence leader, whose family was murdered in 1975? It is hard to imagine. The government would also face heavy international pressure not to execute her: from India, obviously, but from other countries as well. Human rights organisations would point out that sentencing someone to death after a trial they took no part in, and possibly with no right of appeal, is a particularly egregious violation of fair trial rights.

Yet sparing her carries its own risk: a “Shahbagh on steroids,” with tens of thousands on the streets demanding her execution and serious instability for the government.

So, by offering to return, Hasina makes herself relevant again and hands the government a problem it cannot easily solve, along with the kind of political instability she would be well placed to exploit. That is why her decision is more likely genuine, not just a gesture.

And it explains why the Bangladesh government has responded the way it has. For the last year, since her conviction, it has demanded that India hand Hasina over so she can face the tribunal’s death sentence. Now that she says she will come back on her own, it appears to be refusing to help her do that. On the face of it, this makes no sense. The government says it wants her back, yet now that she is offering to come, it seems to be trying to find reasons to keep her away.

The reason is simple: for all the reasons stated above, Hasina inside Bangladesh is far more dangerous to the government than Hasina in Delhi.

Hasina’s announcement also puts India in a bind. Her voluntary return would, on the face of it, solve New Delhi’s biggest problem with Dhaka: the extradition request it has so far stonewalled. It would not have to hand over a long-standing ally. However, given Dhaka’s insistence on a return under Bangladesh’s extradition treaty with India, something it claims befits a convicted individual, it would seem that Dhaka would blame India for facilitating any attempt by Hasina to return outside the treaty arrangements, creating a reason for new tensions. In addition, it is difficult to see how India would want to be seen as letting a long-time ally walk towards a possible execution, even if it is apparently her own decision.

Meanwhile, Hasina’s presence in India does have a real cost. Her August 2026 press conference in Delhi, where she and her party leaders spread a series of falsehoods and disinformation, derailed preparations for Tarique Rahman’s first visit, which Narendra Modi wants as India tries to repair ties and limit Dhaka’s drift towards Pakistan and China.

The irony is that Dhaka and Delhi may now share an interest: neither really seems to want Hasina back in Bangladesh, and Dhaka’s apparent refusal to give her a passport or travel papers lets India keep her without having to say so.

David Bergman is a journalist who has written about Bangladesh for many years. His X handle is @TheDavidBergman.

articles.title: What is holding back the health sector’s development spending?
articles.excerpt: The health sector in Bangladesh faces a troubling paradox: on the one hand, public hospitals struggle with shortages of medicines, diagnostic equipment and healthcare professionals, while on the other, a substantial portion of the budget allocation remains unutilised.
articles.fullText:
Although it is not unusual for the development expenditure to be generally slower during the first quarter, the above-mentioned figures raise an important question: why has the health ministry struggled to translate its budget allocations into implementable programmes? The explanation lies in interconnected structural challenges: discontinuation of the Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp), changes in government and policy priorities, inadequate institutional capacity, and delays in preparing and approving Development Project Proposals (DPPs).

For more than two decades, Bangladesh has implemented major development activities through successive Health, Population and Nutrition Sector Programmes (HPNSPs) under SWAp. These programmes provided a common planning and financing framework, with operational plans covering immunisation, disease control, maternal and child health, family planning, nutrition, and the strengthening of the healthcare system. The fourth programme ended in June 2024, and the proposed fifth programme was discontinued during the interim government . The decision reflected concerns about duplication, overlapping management structures, inefficiencies and weak accountability.

The transition has changed not only how projects are financed, but also how they must be planned and managed. Under the replacement arrangement, development activities are increasingly expected to be implemented through individual DPPs. Preparing these proposals requires technical design, costing, feasibility assessment, procurement planning and multiple approvals. While some DPPs have been prepared and approved, the broader pipeline has not been sufficiently ready for implementation. The fundamental problem here is that the previous programme management structure was discontinued before an equally functional alternative was firmly established.

Changes in government and administrative leadership have brought to the table new policy commitments and development priorities. Reconsidering projects, agreeing on priorities, and translating new commitments into feasible designs take time. The interim administration initiated the shift away from SWAp, while the elected government introduced its own health sector commitments and substantially increased development allocations. However, defining new priorities, reviewing earlier proposals and translating commitments into costed projects require institutional continuity and adequate preparation. The health sector faces competing demands: uninterrupted vaccine administration, essential medicine and contraceptive supplies, maternal and child healthcare, communicable and non-communicable disease control, stronger primary care, disease surveillance, recruitment of health personnel, emergency services, and hospital infrastructure.

The issue is how these priorities are sequenced. Essential services should take priority over less urgent infrastructure investment. A need-based, costed project pipeline must come before or at least accompany budget commitments. Without an agreed, need-based prioritisation framework, implementing agencies may struggle to determine which projects should proceed first. The health ministry needs to distinguish immediate service delivery requirements from medium-term system strengthening and long-term infrastructure investment. The priority should be projects that address urgent population health needs, demonstrate implementation readiness, and protect continuity of essential services.

Preparing a DPP is not simply completing an administrative form. It requires expertise in epidemiology, needs assessment, financial analysis, costing, procurement, monitoring and evaluation, and project management. However, officials under different directorates already carry extensive responsibilities for managing services, personnel, administration, disease outbreaks, procurement and coordination with the ministry and field-level facilities. The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), for example, oversees hospitals, primary healthcare, disease control, planning and research, management information systems, and other technical operations. Similarly, the Directorate General of Family Planning (DGFP) and medical education institutions have their own workloads. Hence, the responsibility of preparing the DPPs may not reasonably be assigned as additional duties without dedicated technical support, clear accountability and sufficient time.

Under SWAp, designated line directors, programme managers and deputy programme managers undertook development programme management responsibilities. After SWAp was discontinued, the ministry abolished these designations in September 2025, removing the previous programme management arrangements. But doing so did not make the need for specialised development planning disappear. The ministry and DGHS have planning functions, but the transition to multiple project-based arrangements requires a stronger, multidisciplinary project preparation capacity. The challenge is not necessarily a shortage of capable officials, but the absence of sufficiently protected time, specialised technical teams, and the institutional arrangement to translate policy priorities into implementable projects. The same problem extends to other implementing agencies, including DGFP and institutions responsible for infrastructure, medical education and specialised services.

A block allocation is a provision for prospective projects, not money that can be spent immediately without the required approvals. Without approved DPPs and appointed project personnel, implementing agencies cannot proceed with many planned procurement and implementation activities, and expenditure will lag even when resources are available on paper. This is particularly relevant to the substantial block allocation in FY2026-27. Routine delays in fund release and budget processing can add to the problem. Delays may subsequently encourage hurried procurement towards the end of the financial year, increasing risks to efficiency and value for money. That would substitute one governance problem for another. Faster expenditure should not come at the expense of quality and accountability.

What the country needs is faster preparation and more disciplined execution, not spending just for the sake of it. The immediate priority must be establishing a dedicated, multidisciplinary project preparation and implementation support team within the health ministry, working closely with DGHS, DGFP, the Planning Commission, and other implementing agencies. The mechanism can bring together health planners, health economists, public health specialists, finance and procurement professionals, and experienced project managers. Development partners and research institutions could provide time-bound technical assistance. Second, the ministry should develop a prioritised, costed project pipeline with clearly assigned responsibilities and timelines for DPP preparation, appraisal, approval and implementation. Existing services requiring uninterrupted financing should be identified first. Clear delegation to DGHS, DGFP and relevant technical agencies, alongside stronger coordination with the Planning Commission and Finance Division, would ease the burden on central policymakers.

Third, senior policymakers and DGHS directors need to provide strategic oversight to undertake technical project preparation by the team. Clear delegation, dedicated project teams, and stronger coordination between planning and implementing agencies are essential. Fourth, quarterly monitoring can track allocations, approvals, fund releases, expenditure and service outcomes. Progress against these milestones can be publicly reported. Last but not the least, development and operating budgets must be better coordinated. New hospitals and equipment investments will yield limited benefits without recurrent financing for staff, maintenance and essential supplies.

That Bangladesh needs greater public investment in healthcare is beyond dispute. But the experience of the July-September period of this fiscal year shows why the ability to plan and deliver matters as much as the size of an allocation. The challenge is not simply to accelerate spending but to establish the structures, expertise and accountability necessary to convert financial resources into quality healthcare. Unless the country invests in the institutional capacity to plan and implement its health budget, larger allocations will hardly meet all healthcare needs.

Dr Rumana Huque is professor in the Department of Economics at Dhaka University and executive director at ARK Foundation.

articles.title: Draft cyber law revisions could still be a tool for silencing dissent
articles.excerpt: If one intends to silence the media, there is no need to put every critical journalist or investigative reporter in jail.
articles.fullText:
Bangladesh knows this all too well. The 2024 uprising was meant to mark a departure from this authoritarian policy that, under the Sheikh Hasina regime, found its most potent expression in the cyber security law. However, attempts to amend the law in recent months have raised fresh doubt about whether the country can decisively break away from that legacy or will end up restoring the tools used to suppress dissent.

In response to consultations with civil society, the government has now reportedly made 12 revisions in the draft cyber law. The revised draft has yet to be released publicly, but from what has been reported, we must admit that some of the changes seem quite positive. Rumour will no longer mean just any unverified information; it should be proven false to qualify as a rumour. Defamation penalties will align with those in the Penal Code of 1860. Journalists and media outlet owners will be granted certain guarantees against being arrested, and provisions allowing the use of mobile courts to investigate certain cybercrimes will be excluded.

However, these concessions still fail to address the basic concerns. The revisions disclosed by officials don’t seem to show the government’s willingness to give up control over speech. The most alarming of them is that the proposed punishment for spreading rumours stays the same: up to 10 years in prison and/or a fine of up to Tk 40 lakh. Even with the narrowed definition, such severe punishment creates a major risk as the authorities decide what counts as false information.

Journalistic practice often involves dealing with allegations that governments deny. Information on corruption, electoral irregularities, and deaths in custody often emerge through unofficial channels because official institutions are historically secretive and lack transparency. Who decides whether a piece of information is actually false? A government accused of something? The police receiving a complaint? The official in question whose reputation is damaged?

Once the state becomes the judge of what is true or not, the ability to check the facts will depend on the state’s approval. Bangladesh knows well what happens when vague cybercrimes become tools of intimidation. According to a study by the Centre for Governance Studies and the TrialWatch initiative of the Clooney Foundation for Justice, 222 cases filed between 2018 and 2023 under the Digital Security Act (DSA) resulted in the criminalisation of 396 journalists. Among the 30 cases that were investigated in-depth, 27 journalists were arrested, half of whom were held for more than a month. Twenty practised self-censorship, and three left journalism forever. Of course, in hindsight, this dataset provides a partial view as the full picture of the total damage caused by the DSA—and its successor, the Cyber Security Act (CSA)—has yet to be established.

But it is clear that successful prosecution was not necessary to hurt someone or enforce censorship. Arrests, uncertainty, expensive legal processes, and reputational damage could do the job. The process that one targeted by the law had to go through became a punishment in itself. That is why the proposed protections for journalists are important but still insufficient. It is good news that the arrests and prosecution of journalists and media owners for publishing information will require prior court approval. But why should ordinary citizens with political views have fewer protections? As Dr Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), noted in his comment on the revisions , protecting journalists but no other citizens may lead to an unfair distinction. Freedom of expression is a constitutional right of every citizen, not just journalists, researchers, activists or politicians.

Another serious gap in the draft is the part on search, seizure and arrest without a warrant (sections 33, 34 and 35), which the revised version has left unaddressed. These provisions may be especially damaging when applied to journalists who keep their sources confidential.

The changes to the provision on blocking content are also inadequate. Authorities will have to notify their decisions within three days and dispose of the application to unblock the content within 15 days. This requirement cannot replace the judicial approval of censorship—notification after censorship is not equivalent to protection from censorship.

Aligning defamation penalties with the Penal Code also seems like a wrong step. Reducing the proposed maximum imprisonment period from five to two years does not solve the main problem: criminal prosecution should not be available for disputes of a reputational nature, which should be resolved through proportional civil remedies.

Moreover, there are concerns about the provisions for cancelling a media organisation’s registration or licence after conviction, especially for an individual’s offence. It is quite excessive and unreasonable to punish the whole institution for the deeds of its members.

Undoubtedly, the government faces certain cybersecurity problems. Cybercrimes like hacking, fraud, sexual exploitation, harassment, blackmailing and even AI-generated abuse require proper legal measures. But protecting citizens from cybercrimes and protecting the government from criticism are completely different goals. The Editors’ Council’s recommendations are more plausible: judicial oversight of arrests, search, seizure, and surveillance; protection of confidential sources; protection of public interest reporting; and protection against penalising media outlets for a single publication.

The government should remove criminal penalties for rumours and defamation, strengthen judicial oversight, and provide protection to all citizens without distinction. Its readiness to revise the draft is good news, but real change would be impossible without renouncing the idea that online criticism is a threat to be controlled.

Above all, Bangladesh cannot, and should not, rely on mere assurances that restrictive laws will not be misused. The DSA and CSA proved how easy it is to transform legal tools into weapons of intimidation. The only test of press freedom is journalists’ ability to investigate and embarrass the government without fear of imprisonment. The country needs an effective cybersecurity law, not another tool for controlling public opinion.

Zillur Rahman , a political analyst, is president at the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) and founding board chair of CGS USA. He hosts ‘Tritiyo Matra’ on Channel i. His X handle is @zillur.
